lesson.title: Keeping Score: The Counter Pattern
lesson.summary: The counter pattern uses a variable that increases by a fixed amount each time a loop runs, letting a program keep a running tally of how many times something happens.
lesson.body:
A huge number of programming problems boil down to a single question: how many times does something happen? How many students passed the test, how many words start with a vowel, how many login attempts failed. None of these answers exist inside a single pass through the data. They have to accumulate across every iteration of a loop, and that accumulation needs somewhere to live that survives from one loop cycle to the next. That somewhere is a counter, a variable created before the loop starts and updated by a fixed amount every time the condition it is tracking is met.

The mechanics rest on two ideas you already know. First, a loop pattern gives you the repeated structure: some block of code that runs once per item or once per condition check. Second, augmented assignment gives you the update step. Writing count += 1 is shorthand for count = count + 1, and it matters here for more than brevity. It reads the current value of count, adds one, and stores the result back in the same variable, which is exactly the read-modify-write cycle a counter depends on. Every single trip through the loop performs that cycle once, and the variable's value after the loop reflects the total number of times the triggering condition was true.

A counter is really a specialized case of a broader idea called the accumulator pattern, where a variable collects a result across a loop. A sum accumulator adds a different amount each time (the next number in a list). A counter accumulator always adds the same fixed amount, usually 1, regardless of what triggered it. That fixed step is what makes counters simple to reason about: you never have to ask 'how much did it change this time,' only 'did it change at all.'

Consider counting how many even numbers appear in a list. The setup initializes count to 0 before the loop begins, then the loop body checks each number and increments count only when the check passes:

numbers = [3, 8, 15, 22, 7, 10]
count = 0
for n in numbers:
    if n % 2 == 0:
        count += 1
print(count)

Trace it by hand. n starts at 3, which is odd, so count stays 0. n becomes 8, which is even, so count becomes 1. n becomes 15, odd, count stays 1. n becomes 22, even, count becomes 2. n becomes 7, odd, count stays 2. Finally n becomes 10, even, count becomes 3. The loop ends and print(count) outputs 3, matching the three even numbers 8, 22, and 10 in the list.

Two mistakes show up constantly with this pattern. Initializing count = 0 inside the loop instead of before it resets the tally on every single iteration, so the final value only ever reflects the last item checked. Forgetting to initialize count at all before referencing it raises a NameError, because Python has no idea what count += 1 should add to. Getting the initialization right, once, outside and before the loop, is what makes the counter pattern reliable for tasks as varied as tallying votes, counting defective parts on an assembly line, or measuring how many characters in a string are digits.
